overview.text: Gold is a chemical element, Au, with atomic number 79. Its yellow color, resistance to corrosion, and ability to be hammered into thin sheets made it valuable for ornaments, coinage, and other objects across many societies. In world history, gold also connected distant trading regions. Caravans crossed the Sahara to exchange West African gold for goods including salt, helping sustain states such as Ghana and Mali. The Mali ruler Mansa Musa carried so much gold on his fourteenth-century pilgrimage that his arrival affected the Cairo market. Later discoveries prompted gold rushes in places including California and Australia. Its physical properties and historical uses explain its lasting importance.

key_facts.text: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word aurum.
Gold is element 79 in the periodic table.
Pure gold is called 24-carat gold.
West African gold was a major commodity in trans-Saharan trade.
Mansa Musa brought substantial gold to Cairo on his 1324–25 pilgrimage.

overview.text: Tulip Mania refers to a burst of speculative trading in tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic during 1636 and 1637. Unusual flowers had become fashionable, and some rare bulbs commanded very high prices. Buyers and sellers also made contracts for bulbs that would be delivered later, so trading could continue while the plants were underground. Prices fell sharply in 1637, leaving disputes over those contracts. The episode became famous through later accounts that portrayed an entire society ruined by irrational buying. Modern historians caution that those dramatic stories drew on satire and exaggeration; the available evidence supports a narrower market frenzy, not a collapse of the Dutch economy.

overview.text: Russia, formally the Russian Federation, stretches across eastern Europe and northern Asia, with Moscow as its capital. Its territory includes the broad plains west of the Ural Mountains and the forests and tundra of Siberia. The country has had several forms of government: an empire ruled by tsars, a revolutionary government after 1917, and then the Soviet era. Tsar Nicholas II abdicated during the February Revolution, and Bolsheviks overthrew the provisional government later that year. Russia became a major constituent republic of the Soviet Union after a civil war. When that union dissolved in 1991, the Russian Federation emerged as an independent state and was recognized as its successor.

overview.text: The Battle of Stalingrad was a major Soviet victory over Nazi Germany in 1942–1943. German troops reached the city on the Volga during an offensive aimed partly at southern Soviet resources. Fighting moved through streets, factories, and ruined buildings while Soviet defenders held parts of the riverbank. In November 1942, the Red Army launched Operation Uranus against the German flanks and encircled the Sixth Army. Attempts to supply the trapped force by air failed, and the remaining troops surrendered by early February 1943. The defeat destroyed a large German field army and helped shift momentum on the Eastern Front toward the Soviet Union.

overview.text: Stalingrad was the name used from 1925 to 1961 for the Russian city now called Volgograd. The city lies along the Volga River and was previously named Tsaritsyn. Under the Stalingrad name it grew into an important Soviet industrial center and became the scene of one of World War II’s most destructive battles. German and Soviet forces fought across the city in 1942–1943, leaving much of it in ruins. The government renamed it Volgograd in 1961. Memorials there still recall the wartime defense, including the large Motherland Calls sculpture on Mamayev Kurgan. The name Stalingrad survives especially in accounts of the battle.

overview.text: Argentina’s Dirty War was the military dictatorship’s campaign of repression against perceived opponents, chiefly from 1976 to 1983. Security forces kidnapped people, held many in secret detention centers, tortured prisoners, and caused thousands to disappear. Victims included political activists as well as people targeted through association or suspicion. Families often received no official account of what had happened. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began publicly demanding answers in 1977, and their white headscarves became a symbol of the search for justice. After civilian rule returned, Argentina formed a commission to investigate disappearances and later pursued prosecutions. A national commission later collected testimony from survivors and relatives of the disappeared.

The dictatorship ended in December 1983.

overview.text: The House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma, was associated with the Abbasid court in Baghdad. Surviving evidence points especially to a royal library and the translation of Persian and other writings into Arabic. Baghdad also supported a much wider scholarly network: translators, physicians, mathematicians, and astronomers worked for caliphs and other patrons. Greek writings reached Arabic readers through several routes, often with the help of Christian scholars working in Syriac. Older accounts sometimes depict one grand academy where all this learning took place, but historians find that picture too simple. The institution matters as part of Baghdad’s lively culture of books and translation, not as the sole source of Abbasid scholarship.

overview.text: Zionism is a modern Jewish national movement that developed in late nineteenth-century Europe and sought a Jewish homeland in the historic Land of Israel, then commonly called Palestine. It arose partly in response to antisemitism and drew on longstanding Jewish ties to that land. Theodor Herzl helped organize political Zionism and convened the first Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897. The British Balfour Declaration of 1917 endorsed a Jewish national home in Palestine; British rule and immigration policies later became contested. The creation of Israel in 1948 fulfilled a central Zionist goal. It followed a United Nations partition proposal amid conflict between Palestinian Arabs and Jews over the land.

overview.text: Hungary is a Central European country whose capital, Budapest, lies on the Danube. Its twentieth-century history included alliance with Nazi Germany, the Holocaust, and Soviet domination after World War II. In 1944 German forces occupied Hungary, and German and Hungarian authorities deported hundreds of thousands of Jews, many to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg and others tried to protect Jews in Budapest. In 1956 a popular uprising challenged Soviet control and the country’s Communist leadership. Soviet troops intervened and crushed it. The revolt became an important symbol of resistance to Soviet rule in Eastern Europe. A later United Nations inquiry described the uprising as a spontaneous movement supported by students, workers, and intellectuals.

overview.text: The Mapuche are Indigenous peoples with a long history in south-central Chile and neighboring parts of Argentina. They resisted Spanish attempts to dominate their homeland during the Arauco War, and later maintained a frontier marked by both conflict and trade. In the nineteenth century, the new Chilean and Argentine states expanded into Mapuche territory through military campaigns. Chile’s occupation and colonization of Araucanía sharply reduced Mapuche control of land and changed community life. Mapuche identity and language, Mapudungun, remain important today, alongside continuing demands connected to land and political recognition. Their history is one of adaptation and persistence as well as resistance to conquest.
